tagline: Coral coasts on the Indian Ocean
overview:
Mozambique stretches down the southeast coast of Africa, a long curve of land facing the Indian Ocean with roughly 2,500 kilometers of beaches, dunes, and coral reefs. It is about twice the size of California and shares borders with Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini, and South Africa. The Zambezi, one of Africa's greatest rivers, crosses the country and spreads into a wide delta before reaching the sea.

About 33 million people live in Mozambique. Portuguese is the official language, left behind by centuries of Portuguese rule, but most families speak an African language such as Makhuwa, Sena, or Changana at home. The capital, Maputo, sits in the far south and keeps wide avenues lined with jacaranda trees, Art Deco buildings, and a fish market where buyers pick their catch and have it grilled on the spot.

Mozambique is a republic with an elected president. Most people farm maize, cassava, and cashews, and fishers work the warm, shallow waters offshore.
landAndNature: Most of Mozambique is low, hot, and flat, a coastal plain that climbs to plateaus and highlands in the north and west, where Mount Binga reaches 2,436 meters on the Zimbabwean border. Rain comes with the summer monsoon between November and April, and tropical cyclones sometimes sweep in off the Indian Ocean. The Bazaruto and Quirimbas archipelagos shelter reefs and seagrass beds where dugongs graze, and whale sharks and manta rays gather off Tofo. Sea turtles nest on the beaches. Inland, Gorongosa National Park, emptied of animals during years of war, has been restocked and now holds elephants, lions, buffalo, and clouds of waterbirds. Baobabs with fat, barrel-like trunks stand in the dry woodlands.
peopleAndCulture: Mozambique's peoples include the Makhuwa, Tsonga, Sena, and Shona, along with Swahili communities on the coast; the north has been Muslim for centuries while the south is largely Christian. Cooking mixes African, Portuguese, Indian, and Arab ideas: grilled piri-piri chicken, prawns, coconut-milk stews called matapa made with cassava leaves and ground peanuts, and Portuguese-style bread rolls. Makonde carvers in the north shape dark ebony into sculptures known worldwide, and masked dancers perform at ceremonies. Marrabenta music, played on homemade guitars, grew up in the neighborhoods of Maputo, and the Chopi people's timbila orchestras of wooden xylophones are recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is everywhere, and Mozambique-born Eusébio became one of the great players of the 1960s.
history: Bantu-speaking farmers settled the region around 2,000 years ago, and by the 900s Swahili merchants on the coast were trading gold, ivory, and enslaved people with Arabia, India, and beyond; Sofala was a famous port. Vasco da Gama landed in 1498, and Portugal took the coast and then the interior, running plantations and forced-labor systems and taking part in the slave trade. A liberation movement, FRELIMO, fought a war from 1964 until independence on June 25, 1975. A civil war followed from 1977 to 1992 that killed about a million people and scattered landmines across the countryside. Peace brought elections and rebuilding, and the economy has grown quickly, though cyclones and poverty remain heavy burdens.
funFacts: Mozambique's flag is the only national flag in the world showing a modern rifle, set beside a hoe and an open book.
Maputo's railway station, finished in the early 1900s with a green dome and wrought iron, is often called one of the world's most beautiful.
Mozambique joined the Commonwealth in 1995, the first member that had never been part of the British Empire.
The Ilha de Moçambique, a coral island barely three kilometers long, served as the colony's capital for almost 400 years.
Cashew trees, brought from Brazil by Portuguese traders, became one of Mozambique's best-known crops.
